questions.q: Which three questions does Jon Acuff suggest asking about a thought?
a: Is it true, is it helpful, and is it kind?
Is it new, is it popular, and is it easy?
Is it fast, is it cheap, and is it safe?
Is it mine, is it fair, and is it necessary?
questions.why: Lesson 1 uses these three tests to catch and discard harmful thinking patterns.

questions.q: What does Acuff mean by a “pocket jury”?
a: A mental exercise where you weigh the evidence for a thought
A group of friends you consult before making decisions
A list of quotes you keep on your phone
A notebook where you record daily complaints
questions.why: Lesson 1 describes presenting evidence to an imagined jury when asking whether a thought is true.

questions.q: Where does the summary suggest starting when inverting an old soundtrack?
a: With thoughts phrased in absolutes like “I must” or “it has to be perfect”
With memories of your earliest childhood
With advice from people who disagree with you
With the goals you have already achieved
questions.why: Lesson 2 says absolute demands are the best place to flip a thought into its opposite.

questions.q: How did Acuff use a borrowed soundtrack to change his writing?
a: He replaced the demand to finish the book at once with a few pages at a time
He repeated a rapper’s line about his life being great
He wrote only when inspiration struck
He asked a friend to set daily word targets
questions.why: Lesson 2 shows Acuff flipping “finish the whole book in one sitting” into finishing a few pages at a time.

questions.q: Why does the summary recommend keeping a symbolic object with you?
a: It reminds you of your new soundtracks and helps them stick
It brings good luck during important meetings
It distracts you whenever you start overthinking
It proves to others that you have changed
questions.why: Lesson 3 explains that an item tied to a memory can anchor the positive thoughts you want to keep.
